\chapter{Quién --- The Asking Word for People}
\label{ch:quien}
\hlchaptermodality{232}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can ask who somebody is.}

I can ask who somebody is.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[quién]{quién — the asking word reserved for people}

\label{lesson:ES-C61-quien}



\begin{quote}
\emph{¿Qué es esto?} asks about a \textbf{thing}.

But you cannot ask \emph{¿Qué es} about a person and expect a name. For people, Spanish keeps a different word entirely.
\end{quote}

\begin{cousinweb}
\begin{quote}
\emph{¿\emph{\textbf{\emph{Quién}} }es?} — Who is it?
\end{quote}

It carries the accent, like every asking word, and it sits between the two marks.

Latin had \emph{\textbf{quis}} for \emph{who} — but the form Spanish kept is \emph{\textbf{quem}}, the shape the word took when it was the \textbf{object} of the sentence. Latin marked that job with an ending; Spanish threw the endings away and was left holding this one form, which then had to do every job. So \emph{quién} is an old object-form doing subject work, and has been since before anyone noticed.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{culture}
The division is simple and it does not bend:

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{} & \textbf{} \\
\midrule
\emph{\textbf{qué}} & things, ideas, anything not a person \\
\emph{\textbf{quién}} & people, and only people \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

English blurs this — \emph{what is that person to you?} is fine English. Spanish will not: if the answer is a person, the question takes \emph{quién}.

And it has a plural, which English does not. If you expect more than one person in the answer, you ask \emph{\textbf{quiénes}}.
\end{culture}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{¿Quién es?}
  \item \emph{¿Qué es esto?}, then \emph{¿Quién es?}, and hear the split
\end{itemize}

\emph{Twice through:}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which asking word is reserved for people? (\emph{\textbf{Quién}}.)

And what do you ask when you expect several? (\emph{\textbf{Quiénes}}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
